platforms.name: NVIDIA DGX Spark (GB10 Grace Blackwell)

gpu_usable_memory.details: No fixed GPU carve-out. NVIDIA: 'Unlike other vendors, which use a fixed carve-out for the iGPU in the shared memory, we utilize a dynamic unified memory architecture (UMA)'. The GPU can allocate what Linux has available (MemAvailable; swap can free more). Users' `free` output on NVIDIA's forum shows 121 GiB total on the Founders Edition and some OEM units, about 119-119.7 GiB on others (firmware-dependent). Subtract OS/desktop working set and page cache (NVIDIA's FAQ suggests dropping caches if allocations fail). cudaMemGetInfo under-reports allocatable memory and nvidia-smi shows 'Memory-Usage: Not Supported' (NVIDIA known issues). Calculator model: usable_gpu ~= OS-visible total (~119.7-121.7 GiB) minus OS/apps; NVIDIA publishes no fixed figure.

official_price.config: DGX Spark Founders Edition (128 GB / 4 TB); current NVIDIA MSRP, raised on 2026-02-23 from the $3,999 launch MSRP ('applies to all regions')

Bandwidth: nvidia.com 'Memory Bandwidth 273 GB/s'; NVIDIA hardware doc '256-bit interface, 4266 MHz, 273 GB/s' (256 x 4266 x 2 / 8 = 273). CUDA compute capability 12.1. NVIDIA's docs do not mention Vulkan for GB10, so it is not listed as officially supported, although the llama.cpp Vulkan scoreboard (#10879) has a working 'Nvidia GB10' result. CPU = 20 Arm cores (llama.cpp CPU backend supports ARM NEON). official_price kind is the schema's 'launch-msrp' but the value is NVIDIA's current USD MSRP posted by an NVIDIA employee on NVIDIA's forum; the es-es NVIDIA marketplace was unreachable from this environment.

platforms.name: AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 (Strix Halo, Radeon 8060S), 128 GB systems

gpu_usable_memory.details: Windows: AMD Variable Graphics Memory (BIOS/Adrenalin) can dedicate up to 96 GB of a 128 GB system; AMD says the iGPU can technically address 112 GB total including shared memory, with best performance when workloads stay within 96 GB. Default is 512 MB dedicated and about 64.3 GB total graphics-addressable. On 64 GB systems AMD cites a 48 GB VGM max, i.e. 0.75 of RAM in both stated cases (fraction is inferred from those two cases, not a published formula). Linux: GPU allocations are GTT-backed; the default GTT limit is about 50% of RAM, raisable via /sys/module/ttm/parameters/pages_limit (amd-ttm --set); AMD's example sets 100 GB on a system reporting 125.65 GB and recommends a small BIOS VRAM carve-out (e.g. 0.5 GB). AMD states no Linux maximum. Kernel minimums: Ubuntu 24.04 HWE 6.17.0-19.19~24.04.2, OEM 6.14.0-1018, other distros 6.18.4.

platforms.notes: Bandwidth: AMD blogs state '256 GB/s'; cross-check 256-bit LPDDR5x x 8000 MT/s / 8 = 256 GB/s (equivalently 4 channels x 8000 MT/s x 8 bytes). Power: spec page 'Default TDP 55W | AMD Configurable TDP (cTDP) 45-120W'; power_w = 120 W is the cTDP maximum (SoC package power, OEM-set), not wall power. The chip ships with 32-128 GB; this entry is the 128 GB configuration. ROCm on Windows is PyTorch-only ('Only Pytorch is currently available on Windows - the rest of the ROCm stack is only supported on Linux'). AMD itself uses Vulkan llama.cpp on Windows. Sold only as OEM systems, so official_price is null.

platforms.name: Desktop CPU, dual-channel DDR5-5600 (reference: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X)
platforms.notes: Bandwidth = channels x MT/s x 8 bytes per transfer = 2 x 5600 x 8 MB/s = 89.6 GB/s. The formula reproduces AMD's own published figure for EPYC 9004 (12 x 4800 x 8 = 460.8 GB/s, listed on amd.com as 'Per Socket Mem BW 460.8 GB/s'); AMD does not publish a bandwidth row for Ryzen desktop parts. AMD's 9950X page caps the speed by DIMM population: '2x1R DDR5-5600, 2x2R DDR5-5600, 4x1R DDR5-3600, 4x2R DDR5-3600', so filling four slots drops the rated speed to DDR5-3600 = 57.6 GB/s. Max memory 256 GB ('Max. Memory 256 GB'); installed RAM is a user input (memory_options_gb null). power_w is the CPU 'Default TDP 170W' of the reference part, not system power. XMP/EXPO overclocked kits exceed the rated speed and are out of spec. No clean llama-bench tg128 result for a dense model on a dual-channel DDR5 desktop was found in the llama.cpp threads, so this tier has no direct calibration point (the closest is a DDR4-3200 dual-channel laptop at k=0.52).

platforms.name: Server CPU, 12-channel DDR5-4800 per socket (reference: AMD EPYC 9004 'Genoa')
platforms.notes: amd.com lists for both EPYC 9124 and EPYC 9654: 'System Memory Type DDR5 | Memory Channels 12 | System Memory Specification Up to 4800 MT/s | Per Socket Mem BW 460.8 GB/s'. That equals 12 x 4800 x 8 / 1000, the same channels x MT/s x 8 bytes formula used for the desktop entry. Bandwidth is per socket. In llama.cpp discussion #11733 (fairydreaming, #discussioncomment-12240601) dual-socket runs with --numa distribute reached 181-183% of single-socket tg128 on dense Llama-3.1-70B F16, but only 102-111% on DeepSeek-R1 (MoE); likwid-bench measured 73-92% of the theoretical channel bandwidth. power_w left null because TDP depends on SKU: amd.com lists 'Default TDP 200W' (EPYC 9124, 16 cores) and 'Default TDP 360W' (EPYC 9654, 96 cores). Installed RAM is a user input (memory_options_gb null); every one of the 12 channels must be populated to get the full 460.8 GB/s. Price: AMD lists 1kU tray pricing for CPUs only (e.g. '1kU Pricing 1083 USD' for 9124), which is not a system price, so official_price is null.

calibration.formula: ceiling_tps = memory_bandwidth_gbps / model_size_gb; size_gb = llama-bench size (GiB) x 1.073741824; k = tg128 / ceiling_tps
